Guided Inquiry

The wall

An outside wall in winter — 20 °C inside, 0 °C outside. It is built in three layers: 10 cm brick, 5 cm insulation, 2 cm plaster. The arrows show heat current through the wall. Look at the red temperature profile. Where is it steep, and where is it shallow?

Predict

You want to lose less heat. You can double one layer's thickness. Which saves more heat?

Now try it

Drag the insulation slider in the sidebar from 5 cm → 10 cm and watch the heat rate. Then reset it, and try doubling the brick instead (10 → 20 cm).

The insulation slice is thin but steep — it takes almost the whole 20 °C drop. That is why doubling it matters. The brick is thick but shallow.

The rule

In series, thermal resistances add: R = L/(kA), same shape as electrical resistors. The heat current
H = ΔT / Rtotal
is the same in every layer — so the temperature drop across each layer is proportional to its own R.

Thin bad conductor beats thick good conductor. That is why houses have insulation, not extra brick.

Conduction Through a Wall

01

At a glance

A winter wall is built in three layers: brick, insulation and plaster. The inside is held at 20 °C and the outside at 0 °C, so heat flows through the layers one after another. The sim lets you change each layer's thickness and read off the heat current.

What you'll learn

  • How the thermal resistance R = L/(kA) of a layer follows from its thickness and its conductivity.
  • How the resistances of layers in series combine to set the heat current H.
  • How the temperature drop across each layer is related to its resistance.
The three layers, drawn to scale in thickness at the sim's opening values.

What's on screen

  • The wall: three coloured layers with their thickness written beneath, brick on the inside, plaster on the outside.
  • Red line: the temperature at each point of the wall, from the inside face to the outside face.
  • Yellow chevrons: the heat current, drifting from inside to outside.
  • Heat readouts in the sidebar: the heat rate H and the total resistance.
See itStart with the opening wall: 10 cm brick, 5 cm insulation, 2 cm plaster. Watch for: the red line running from the INSIDE 20 °C face to the OUTSIDE 0 °C face.

03

Heat current through one layer is kAΔT/L

In steady state the temperatures no longer change with time, and heat passes through a layer at a constant rate H, in watts. Fourier's law gives it for a layer of conductivity k, area A and thickness L, with a temperature difference ΔT across it:

H = kAΔT / L = ΔT / R, R = L / (kA)
R is the thermal resistance of the layer, in K/W. It plays the role of electrical resistance, with H as the current and ΔT as the voltage.

A thicker layer has a larger R, and a better conductor has a smaller one. As a single-layer example, 10 cm of brick (k = 0.8 W/m·K) over 1 m² has R = 0.10 / (0.8 × 1) = 0.125 K/W. If the whole 20 K fell across that brick alone, it would pass 20 / 0.125 = 160 W.

04

Resistances in series add

In the wall, the same heat passes through the brick, then the insulation, then the plaster, like resistors in series. Their resistances add, and the current follows from the total:

Rtot = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, H = (Tin − Tout) / Rtot
The sim computes every number from these two relations.
Layerk (W/m·K)L (cm)R = L/(kA) (K/W)
Brick0.8100.125
Insulation0.0451.250
Plaster0.1520.133
Total1.508

So H = 20 K / 1.508 K/W = 13.26 W. The insulation holds 83 % of the total resistance, although it is the thinnest of the three big layers.

See itUse the opening wall: 10 cm brick, 5 cm insulation, 2 cm plaster. Watch for: Total resistance 1.508 K/W and Heat rate H 13.26 W in the sidebar.
05

Each layer takes a drop in proportion to its R

In steady state heat cannot pile up inside a layer, so the same H leaves a layer as enters it. The same H crosses every layer, and the temperature drop across layer i is

ΔTi = H Ri
A bigger R means a bigger drop, which is a steeper stretch of the temperature line.

With H = 13.26 W the drops are 1.66 °C across the brick, 16.57 °C across the insulation and 1.77 °C across the plaster. They sum to 20 °C. The two interfaces sit at 18.34 °C and 1.77 °C. Each layer passes the same current, as the check kAΔT/L = 13.26 W confirms for all three.

See itUse the opening wall again. Watch for: the interface labels 18.3 °C and 1.8 °C, and the chevrons drifting at one speed in every layer.
06

Doubling the largest R cuts H the most

Thickening a layer adds only that layer's own R to the total. Doubling the 5 cm of insulation adds another 1.250 K/W, so Rtot rises from 1.508 to 2.758 K/W and H falls from 13.26 W to 7.25 W. That removes 45 % of the heat loss.

Doubling the 10 cm of brick adds only 0.125 K/W. Rtot rises to 1.633 K/W and H falls to 12.25 W, a cut of 8 %. The same doubling pays very differently, because what matters is how large the added R is compared with the total already there.

See itDouble the insulation to 10 cm. Watch for: Heat rate H 7.25 W and Total resistance 2.758 K/W, with the insulation taking about 18 °C of the drop.
07

Thickness alone does not set R

R = L/(kA) has the conductivity k in the denominator, so the material counts as much as the thickness. Brick conducts 20 times better than this insulation, with k = 0.8 against 0.04 W/m·K. A centimetre of brick adds 0.0125 K/W, and a centimetre of insulation adds 0.25 K/W, which is 20 times more.

The 5 cm of insulation therefore resists as much as 100 cm of brick. A thin layer of a poor conductor can outweigh a thick layer of a good one, which is why a wall gets its insulation from a thin low-k layer and not from more brick.

See itDouble the brick to 20 cm instead. Watch for: Heat rate H 12.25 W, barely below the 13.26 W you started with.
08

Where it matters

  • Houses. Cavity and loft insulation put a thin layer of low-k material in series with brick, concrete and plaster, and it supplies most of the resistance.
  • Double glazing. Two panes enclose a thin layer of still air. Air conducts poorly, so that gap adds a large R to the series.
  • Layered clothing. Several thin layers trap air, and the resistances add.
  • Electronics. The same series rule sizes the heat sink path from a chip to the air, where each joint adds its own R.
09

Summary

In one line. The heat current through a layered wall is set by the temperature difference and by the total thermal resistance of its layers.

Key points

  • One layer: H = kAΔT/L = ΔT/R, with R = L/(kA).
  • Layers in series add: Rtot = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ and H = ΔT/Rtot.
  • H is the same in every layer, so ΔTi = H Ri.

Common mix-ups

  • "Thicker always means less heat loss." Thickness is only one factor in R = L/(kA). The conductivity k counts as well.
  • "Heat is used up as it crosses a layer." In steady state the same H leaves each layer as enters it.
  • "The layer with the biggest temperature drop passes the most heat." Every layer passes the same H. The biggest drop marks the biggest R.

Things to try on your own

  • Set insulation to 1 cm and find how many degrees it now takes, then compare with the 16.57 °C it took at 5 cm.
  • Set the brick to its 25 cm maximum and compare H with the 7.25 W that 10 cm of insulation gives.
  • Predict H for brick 10, insulation 5, plaster 4 from Rtot, then check it.
